avoid.reason: Europe’s pickpocket capital — La Rambla, the Gothic Quarter, Barceloneta beach and metro line 3 are hotspots.
Parts of El Raval feel edgy after dark — keep valuables secure.

hood_desc: The atmospheric medieval old town of narrow winding alleys, hidden squares and the cathedral. Ideal for visitors who want history, character and a central location on foot.
The elegant grid-plan district showcasing Gaudi masterpieces, wide avenues and upscale shopping. Best for those wanting modernist architecture and stylish, spacious streets.
A charming, village-like bohemian neighborhood with leafy plazas, indie shops and a local festive spirit. Suits travelers seeking an authentic, laid-back and creative vibe.
A fashionable medieval quarter of trendy boutiques, tapas bars and the Picasso Museum. Great for those wanting historic streets with a chic, lively edge.
A former fishing quarter beside the beach, full of seafood restaurants and a lively waterfront. Perfect for beach lovers wanting sand, sea and paella close to the center.

water.note: Tap water is safe, though some visitors find the taste strong and prefer bottled water.

transit.pay: Buy a T-Casual (10 trips, ~€12/$13) or a Hola BCN tourist card (unlimited rides for 2-5 days, from about €18/$19) at metro machines, TMB stores, or airport kiosks; contactless bank-card tap-in is being rolled out network-wide. A single ticket costs €2.55 (~$2.75).
transit.hours: Metro runs about 5am-midnight (Fri/eve-of-holiday until 2am, all night Saturdays); night buses cover the rest of the network.

landmarks: Sagrada Família
Gaudí's unfinished, spire-studded basilica is Barcelona's most photographed symbol and a UNESCO World Heritage masterpiece of Catalan Modernisme.
Park Güell
A whimsical, mosaic-covered public park designed by Gaudí offering fairy-tale architecture and sweeping views over the city.
Casa Batlló
Gaudí's surreal, skeletal-balconied facade on Passeig de Gràcia is one of the most striking and colorful buildings in the world.
Casa Milà (La Pedrera)
Gaudí's undulating stone facade and sculptural rooftop chimneys make this UNESCO-listed building an unmistakable icon of organic Modernista design.
Barcelona Cathedral
The Gothic Quarter's soaring cathedral, with its cloister of geese and rooftop views, epitomizes Barcelona's medieval heart.
Palau de la Música Catalana
A dazzling Art Nouveau concert hall famed for its stained-glass skylight and ornate facade, ranked among the world's most beautiful auditoriums.
Gothic Quarter (Barri Gòtic)
A labyrinth of medieval stone streets and squares that forms the atmospheric historic core of old Barcelona.
Montjuïc Castle
A hilltop fortress overlooking the port and city, prized for panoramic photography and its commanding views of the Mediterranean.
La Rambla
Barcelona's famous tree-lined pedestrian boulevard, bustling with street performers, markets, and cafés, links Plaça Catalunya to the seafront.
Camp Nou
FC Barcelona's massive stadium is one of the most visited sports landmarks in Europe, iconic to football fans worldwide.

train.note: All international high-speed trains leave from Barcelona Sants. There is no direct night train from Barcelona: the old Paris sleeper was withdrawn in 2013, and the French Intercités de Nuit only gets you to the border area (Latour-de-Carol or Cerbère) with a change of train. Renfe's planned Barcelona-Paris AVE was shelved in 2026, but its Lyon and Marseille services still run.

bus.note: Most long-distance coaches use Barcelona Nord bus station, with some also calling at Sants. ALSA's Morocco coaches cross by ferry at the Strait of Gibraltar - bring your passport and expect a 24h+ trip.

ferry.note: Ferries sail from the Port of Barcelona at Moll de Sant Bertran (Grimaldi Terminal), a short taxi or bus ride from the city centre. Crossings to Italy take roughly 12-20 hours and Morocco sailings around 30 hours; frequencies drop outside summer, so check schedules. Balearia's frequent boats to Mallorca, Menorca and Ibiza are domestic Spanish routes.

half.name: Figueres
